article.headline: GitLab Bets On A Governed AI Software Factory As Sales Climb
article.deck: GitLab is 1.1% past the 55.65 buy point of a five-week cup and inside its buy range, which runs to 58.43.
body: GitLab sells one application that covers the whole job of building software: planning, code, security scans, compliance checks and deployment, under one roof. Its newer pitch is the GitLab Duo Agent Platform, which puts AI agents to work on tasks across planning, development and security alongside human teams.

The growth is in the top line. Revenue rose 21.3% in the July quarter to 286.3 million, and it climbed in every quarter in the table: 244.4 million, 260.4 million, 264.2 million, then 286.3 million. Earnings have not followed. GitLab lost 0.22 a share in the July quarter, after losses of 0.05, 0.02 and 0.03 a share in the three quarters before it.

The market is paying for the revenue. GitLab carries a market value of about 9.38 billion and trades at 54.2 times forward earnings; with losses on the books, it has no trailing P/E. The next report is due Dec. 1.

The stock rose 1.75, or 3.2%, to 56.28 on Friday, on volume 0.69x its 50-day average. It broke out of a five-week cup on Oct. 12, with volume 0.87x average that session. The cup is 20.4% deep, topped on Sept. 2 and bottomed at 44.22 on Sept. 28. The buy point is 55.65 and the buy range runs to 58.43. Nine sessions after the breakout, the close sits 1.1% above the buy point.

The trend is strong. GitLab is 2.8% below its 52-week high of 57.89 and has come a long way from its 52-week low of 18.73. It trades 15.7% above its 50-day line at 48.63 and 67.8% above its 200-day at 33.54. The 21-day exponential average is 52.66, and the stock sits 0.52 ATRs above the 21-day line, nowhere near stretched. GitLab ranks 97 of 99 on the desk's list, and its RS line is 0.9% below its high. Shares are up 50.0% this year and 71.2% over three months.

The news has tracked the AI push. On Oct. 6 the company announced the foundation for what it calls the governed software factory. In September a filing headline reported the CFO's stake dropped by more than 30,000 shares, worth 1.6 million, after the stock hit a 52-week high.
The question for the chart is whether GitLab can hold above 55.65 and push through 57.89; the question for the business is whether the losses narrow as revenue keeps climbing.
article.watch: Whether GitLab holds the 55.65 buy point and clears its 57.89 high before the Dec. 1 report.

article.headline: CrowdStrike Surges 8.2% As Evercore Survey Points To Stronger Cyber Demand
article.deck: CrowdStrike bounced off its 50-day line but has no base on the desk's chart, so there is no buy point until one forms.
body: CrowdStrike jumped 19.63, or 8.2%, to 257.57 on Friday, trading 1.31x its 50-day average volume. The gain came off the 50-day line at 234.80. The desk's chart shows no base, so the stock has no buy point and no buy range.

CrowdStrike is 10.3% below its 52-week high of 286.99. It now trades 9.7% above its 50-day line and 57.4% above its 200-day at 163.61. The 21-day exponential average is 247.34, and the session's range touched it, 0.0 ATRs from the 21-day line. CrowdStrike ranks 97 of 99 on the desk's list, and its RS line is 5.3% below its high. Shares are up 119.8% this year and 106.0% over 12 months.

In the July quarter CrowdStrike earned 0.01 a share on revenue of 1.47 billion, up 25.8%. Revenue rose each quarter in the table, from 1.23 billion to 1.31 billion, 1.39 billion and 1.47 billion. Earnings in the three prior quarters were 0.03, 0.04 and -0.04 a share. The market value is about 263.7 billion and the forward P/E is 159.9. The next report is due Dec. 1.

Friday's headlines said CrowdStrike and Palo Alto jumped as an Evercore survey flagged stronger cybersecurity demand. Another headline asked what CrowdStrike is asking with a reported $500 million security deal.
A new base below the 286.99 high would give the stock a buy point; a break of the 50-day line would undo Friday's bounce.
article.watch: Whether a new base forms below the 286.99 high while the stock holds its 50-day line at 234.80.

corner.topic: Reading a cup with handle: depth, length, the handle's shakeout, and where the buy point sits
corner.headline: Reading A Cup: Depth, Length, The Handle And The Buy Point
corner.deck: ExxonMobil's 27-week cup, with a 176.51 buy point, shows how to measure the pattern and where the entry sits.
body: A cup with handle is the most common base among stocks that go on to lead, and it is also the one most often misread. Four things decide whether a cup is sound: how deep it is, how long it took, whether a handle formed and how it behaved, and where the buy point sits. ExxonMobil's current chart answers each of those questions.

Start with depth. Measure from the left-side high to the low of the cup. Exxon topped on March 30, 2026, at 176.41 and bottomed at 134.95 on June 25, a decline of 23.5%. O'Neil's rule is that most sound cups correct roughly 12% to 33%. Exxon sits in the middle of that span. A cup much deeper than that, in a market that did not fall as hard, says the stock was under real pressure and has more overhead supply to work through on the way back up.

Then length. A cup with handle should take at least seven weeks to form, counting the handle. Exxon's cup took 27 weeks. A longer base is not a flaw; it gives the stock time to shake out holders who bought near the top and want out at breakeven. A cup that forms in three or four weeks has not done that work.

The shape matters too. The bottom should be a rounded U, not a sharp V. A rounded bottom means the stock spent weeks near its lows, wearing out sellers, before it turned. Exxon took from March 30 to June 25 to find its low and then climbed back to the rim before the Oct. 14 breakout.

The handle is the last shakeout. After the right side of the cup rises close to the old high, the stock often pulls back for a week or more. A proper handle drifts lower, forms in the upper half of the base, and stays above the 10-week line. It should not correct more than about 10% to 12%. The handle shakes out the last weak holders before the stock moves. When a handle forms, the buy point is its high plus ten cents. When the stock runs straight up the right side without one, as the desk's data shows for Exxon, the buy point is the cup's high plus ten cents.

For Exxon that gave a buy point of 176.51: the 176.41 rim plus ten cents. The buy range runs 5% above that, to 185.34. Exxon closed through 176.51 on Oct. 14, with volume 1.0x its 50-day average that session, and on Friday it closed at 183.21, 3.8% above the buy point and still inside the range.

What goes wrong without these rules is predictable. Buying the stock in the middle of the right side, well below the 176.41 rim, means buying into the supply left by everyone who bought near the March 30 top. Buying well past 185.34 means paying up for a move that has already happened. The rules of depth, length and the buy point put the entry at the spot where the stock has proved itself and the risk is smallest.
takeaways: Measure depth from the left-side high to the cup's low; most sound cups correct about 12% to 33%.
A cup with handle needs at least seven weeks; Exxon's took 27.
A handle should drift lower in the upper half of the base and correct no more than about 10% to 12%.
The buy point is the handle's high plus ten cents, or the cup's high plus ten cents when there is no handle.
The buy range ends 5% above the buy point; past that, wait for a new base or a pullback to a moving average.
